1:3.t: Ephesus: see Acts 19. 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus are often called the Pastoral Letters, written to Paul's co-workers about leading churches.

1:10.t: "Those practicing homosexuality": the KJV's "them that defile themselves with mankind"; Greek arsenokoitai. See 1 Corinthians 6:9.

2:7.t: "In Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

2:9.t: "Elaborate hairstyles": the KJV's "broided hair", braided hair woven with gold and jewels, a sign of wealth.

2:11.t: Christians understand these verses differently: as a lasting restriction on women teaching or holding authority over men in the church, or as instructions for a particular situation in Ephesus involving false teaching. Verse 15 is difficult; "saved through childbearing" may refer to the birth of the Messiah, to women's ordinary calling, or to being kept safe through childbirth.

3:2.t: "Faithful to his wife": the KJV's "the husband of one wife", literally "a one-woman man". It may forbid polygamy, remarriage, or unfaithfulness; most take it as requiring marital faithfulness.

3:12.t: "Faithful to his wife": the KJV's "the husband of one wife", literally "a one-woman man". It may forbid polygamy, remarriage, or unfaithfulness; most take it as requiring marital faithfulness.

3:3.t: "Not greedy for money": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words in this verse.

3:11.t: "Their wives": the KJV's reading; the Greek gynaikes can also mean "women", that is, women deacons.

3:16.t: "God": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "He who". Either way, the line refers to Christ.

"Mystery" (Greek mysterion): see Matthew 13:11. The rest of the verse appears to be an early hymn about Christ. "Vindicated" (Greek edikaiothe): the KJV's "justified", shown to be in the right, by the Spirit raising Him from the dead.

4:14.t: "The body of elders": the KJV's "the presbytery".

5:9.t: "Over sixty": the KJV's "threescore years old". "Faithful to her husband": the KJV's "the wife of one man"; see 3:2.

5:17.t: "Double honor": probably respect and also financial support (5:18).

5:18.t: Quotations of Deuteronomy 25:4 and Luke 10:7. Paul calls both "Scripture".

5:21.t: "The Lord Jesus Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Christ Jesus".

6:5.t: "Withdraw yourself from such people": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

6:7.t: "It is certain": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

6:20.t: "What is falsely called knowledge": the KJV's "science falsely so called"; Greek gnosis, knowledge, perhaps an early form of the movement later called Gnosticism.

1:15.t: "Trustworthy saying" (Greek pistos ho logos): the KJV's "faithful saying", a formula found five times in the Pastoral Letters, perhaps introducing well-known Christian sayings.

2:4.t: "Wants all people to be saved": God's desire. Christians differ on how this relates to His choosing (see Romans 9), but all agree it grounds prayer and preaching for everyone.

2:5.t: "One mediator" (Greek mesites): a go-between who brings two parties together. Christ, both God and man, is the only one.

3:8.t: "Deacons" (Greek diakonoi): servants, ministers. See Acts 6:2-4 and Romans 16:1.

4:1.t: "Things taught by demons" (Greek didaskaliais daimonion): the KJV's "doctrines of devils". See Matthew 4:24.

4:10.t: "Savior of all people, and especially of those who believe": readers understand "Savior" here as God's care and preservation of all people, or as His offer of salvation to all, received by those who believe.

6:6.t: "Godliness with contentment" (Greek eusebeia meta autarkeias): see Philippians 4:11.

6:10.t: "A root of all kinds of evil" (Greek rhiza panton ton kakon): the KJV's "the root of all evil". The Greek has no article; love of money is a source of every kind of evil, not the only one. It is the love of money, not money itself.

6:15.t: One of the New Testament's great descriptions of God, perhaps from early worship.
